definitions.definition: A complete change in the basic way scientists think about a whole field, not just a small fix.
definitions.example: Like switching from thinking the Earth is flat to knowing it's round.

definitions.definition: The idea that because all past scientific theories were eventually proven wrong, we should expect our current theories to be wrong too.
definitions.example: If every phone you've owned broke after a year, you'd expect your new phone to break too.

definitions.definition: Reasons based on past experiences to believe something will happen again.
definitions.example: If the sun has risen every day of your life, you have inductive grounds to think it will rise tomorrow.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven wrong by an experiment or observation.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan proves it wrong.

definitions.definition: Logically consistent and making sense as a whole.
definitions.example: A story is coherent if all the details fit together without contradictions.

definitions.definition: A scientist who proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun, not the other way around.
definitions.example: Before Copernicus, people thought the Sun went around the Earth.

definitions.definition: A chemist who discovered oxygen and ended the idea of phlogiston.
definitions.example: He showed that burning things uses oxygen from the air.

definitions.definition: A scientist who proved that germs cause disease, not bad air.
definitions.example: He showed that washing hands stops infections.

definitions.definition: An experiment that showed there is no 'aether' that light travels through.
definitions.example: It proved that light doesn't need a medium like sound needs air.

definitions.definition: A physicist who developed the theory of relativity, changing how we understand gravity and time.
definitions.example: He showed that time can slow down when you move very fast.

definitions.definition: The theory that the universe began from a single point and has been expanding ever since.
definitions.example: Like a balloon being inflated from a tiny dot.

definitions.definition: The theory that Earth's outer shell is made of moving plates that cause earthquakes and mountains.
definitions.example: The continents drift like rafts on a slow-moving ocean of rock.

definitions.definition: The current theory that describes all known particles and forces except gravity.
definitions.example: It's like a periodic table for the smallest building blocks of matter.

definitions.definition: A book arguing that science changes through sudden revolutions, not gradual steps.
definitions.example: Like switching from flip phones to smartphones overnight.

definitions.definition: A book arguing that science works by trying to prove theories wrong, not by proving them right.
definitions.example: You can't prove all swans are white, but you can prove they aren't by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: The argument that because past theories were replaced, current ones will be too.
definitions.example: Every map of the world from 500 years ago is wrong, so our maps today will also be wrong someday.

definitions.definition: The idea that God created the rules of logic and reason.
definitions.example: Like a game designer who creates the rules of a board game.

definitions.definition: The idea that God created the physical universe.
definitions.example: Like an author who writes a story and creates its world.

definitions.definition: An ancient model of the universe with Earth at the center and everything else orbiting it.
definitions.example: Like thinking you are the center of the solar system.

definitions.definition: An ancient theory that objects move because of their 'nature' or purpose.
definitions.example: Saying a rock falls because it wants to be on the ground.

definitions.definition: A made-up substance that scientists once thought was released when things burn.
definitions.example: Like thinking a fire releases 'fire-stuff' instead of using oxygen.

definitions.definition: The old belief that diseases spread through 'bad air' or smells.
definitions.example: Like thinking a stinky swamp causes malaria.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical invisible substance that scientists thought light waves traveled through.
definitions.example: Like thinking sound needs air, so light must need something too.

definitions.definition: The belief that everything happens because of a chain of causes and could not have happened any other way.
definitions.example: Like a row of dominoes falling one after another with no choice.

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that describes how very tiny things like atoms and electrons behave.
definitions.example: At this scale, particles can be in two places at once until you look at them.

definitions.definition: The idea that gravity is caused by massive objects bending the fabric of space and time.
definitions.example: Like a heavy ball on a trampoline making a dip that other balls roll into.

definitions.definition: The old theory that the universe has always existed and looks the same forever.
definitions.example: Like a river that always has water but never changes.

definitions.definition: Faint radiation left over from the Big Bang that fills the entire universe.
definitions.example: Like the afterglow of a giant explosion that we can still detect.

definitions.definition: Tiny particles that are the building blocks of protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: Like LEGO bricks that make up bigger pieces of matter.

definitions.definition: Particles that 'glue' quarks together inside protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: Like the glue that holds LEGO bricks together.

definitions.definition: The arrangement of particles smaller than an atom.
definitions.example: Like the parts inside a tiny machine that you can't see with your eyes.

definitions.definition: Things made up of smaller parts.
definitions.example: A sandwich is a composite of bread, meat, and cheese.

definitions.definition: Newton's ideas that space and time are fixed and the same for everyone.
definitions.example: Thinking that one second is the same length for everyone everywhere.

definitions.definition: The theory that the universe has no beginning or end and looks the same at all times.
definitions.example: Like a movie that loops forever with no start or finish.

definitions.definition: Reasoning from specific examples to a general rule.
definitions.example: If you see three black dogs, you might inductively think all dogs are black.

definitions.definition: The idea that we can only know reality through the models our brains create, not directly.
definitions.example: Like seeing the world through a video game screen and thinking the game is the real world.

definitions.definition: Basic assumptions you have to accept before you can start reasoning or investigating.
definitions.example: Before doing a science experiment, you assume the laws of physics won't change mid-experiment.

definitions.definition: The assumption that the laws of nature are the same everywhere and at all times.
definitions.example: Believing that gravity will work tomorrow the same way it works today.

definitions.definition: Reasoning from specific observations to general conclusions.
definitions.example: Seeing the sun rise every morning and concluding it always will.

definitions.definition: The mental abilities we use to think, reason, and understand.
definitions.example: Your memory, attention, and logic skills are cognitive faculties.

definitions.definition: Someone who believes that nature is all that exists and there is no supernatural.
definitions.example: A naturalist thinks the universe came from nothing and has no creator.

definitions.definition: More likely to help an organism survive and reproduce.
definitions.example: Being fast is evolutionarily superior for a rabbit trying to escape a fox.

definitions.definition: Someone who believes in a personal God who created the universe.
definitions.example: A Christian, Muslim, or Jew is a theist.

definitions.definition: The idea that the universe's laws seem fine-tuned for life because we exist to observe them.
definitions.example: If the universe were different, we wouldn't be here to notice it.

definitions.definition: Putting off an answer or explanation instead of giving a real one.
definitions.example: Saying 'we'll figure it out later' instead of answering now.

definitions.definition: A major change in how people think about a topic.
definitions.example: Going from believing the Earth is flat to knowing it's round.

definitions.definition: The process of moving toward a common point or agreement.
definitions.example: Several paths leading to the same destination.
